doc.title: Joseph Daley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 18, 2018

title: Bebop, swing and dancing
summary: Dancing to bop and avant-garde music, extending tradition.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: Right. That’s exactly what has happened. And you know, bop was, people said bop wasn’t, I mean here, the description they gave for bop, bop wasn’t for dancing, well that’s not true. I mean if you see the people doing the lindy hop and all that stuff, you know, at those very fast tempos, you know, so people danced to bop just like they did to swing. It’s just that swing was, the tempos of swing were not as fast as the tempos for bop. So you had to have some serious dancing skill to dance to bebop, whereas dancing to swing, you could just get your partner and just go back and forth. It’s a different tradition and a different generation, a generational thing. But dancing was definitely part of things that you could do with bop, and there’s dancing in the stuff that we do, you can definitely dance to it too, once we get down a groove and everything. And if you go to a thing like the Vision Festival you’ll see like Patricia Parker dancing to all kinds of avante garde, so-called avante garde music and everything. So you can dance to everything. And like I said, we just extended the tradition. We’re not abandoning it and we love Duke Ellington and Thelonious Monk and all those great musicians just as much as the people that play the tradition also.
